name: What ended the Late Bronze Age world around 1177 BCE?

positions.claim: No single blow: drought, famine, earthquakes, raiders and broken trade hit an interlocked system of palaces at once, and each failure made the next one worse.
positions.mech: Interdependence turned local shocks into a chain reaction across Greece, Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt.
for: Destructions cluster in a few decades across many kingdoms
Ugarit's letters mention famine, enemy ships and missing allies at once
The Hittites depended on imported grain
against: 'Systems collapse' can explain anything and is hard to test
Dates of many destructions are loose, so 'simultaneous' may be decades apart

positions.claim: A centuries-long dry spell, with a severe three-year drought around 1198-1196 BCE, cut harvests and drove people to move and fight.
positions.mech: Less rain, smaller grain surplus, hungry cities and mobile populations.
for: Pollen from coastal Syria and the Sea of Galilee shows drying around 1200 BCE
Tree rings from Gordion show three very dry years before Hattusa fell
Grain-shortage letters from Hatti
against: Some proxies are local and loosely dated
Egypt and Assyria lived through the same climate

positions.claim: Barbarian infantry with javelins and long slashing swords learned to beat chariot armies, so the palaces lost their military monopoly.
positions.mech: New weapons and tactics let raiders defeat the elite chariot corps.
for: Naue II swords and new armour spread around 1200 BCE
Palace texts show heavy investment in chariots
against: Chariots stayed in use for centuries after 1200 BCE
Little direct evidence of the tactics Drews proposes

positions.claim: Migrating warrior coalitions from the Aegean and Anatolia overran the coastal kingdoms.
positions.mech: Raids and invasion by sea and land.
for: Medinet Habu names peoples who 'made a conspiracy in their islands'
Ugarit's last letters describe enemy ships
against: Egyptian royal inscriptions are propaganda
Many destroyed sites show no sign of foreign attackers

positions.claim: The palace elites fell, but many towns, villages and trades went on; the 'collapse' is partly an artefact of how archaeologists read burned layers.
positions.mech: A political collapse of thin elites, with regional resilience and reorganisation.
for: Many sites blamed on the Sea Peoples show no destruction
Cyprus and Phoenician cities recovered quickly
Assyria and Egypt survived
against: Writing, palaces and monumental building really did vanish from Greece and Hatti
Population in Greece fell sharply

state: Most specialists now accept a multi-causal crisis with climate as a real stressor; the argument is over weights, timing and how total the collapse was.
settle: Tightly dated destruction layers across many sites, matched to annually resolved climate records from the same regions, would show whether drought came first and where.
fun: Five great powers, one generation, and then four centuries without writing in Greece: was it drought, raiders, earthquakes, or all of them at once?

name: Why did foragers become farmers?

positions.claim: Ice Age climate was too unstable for farming to pay; the steady, CO2-richer Holocene made it possible and then competitive.
positions.mech: Stable climate and higher plant productivity, with the Younger Dryas as a push.
for: Farming arose independently in several regions within a few millennia of 9700 BCE
No farming anywhere in the previous 100,000 years
against: Climate explains when, not why particular people adopted it
Some regions took thousands of years to adopt it

positions.claim: Foragers had filled the world by the end of the Ice Age; farming was a reluctant way to feed more people from the same land.
positions.mech: More mouths, fewer wild resources, intensification.
for: Early farming meant more work and worse health, so people needed a push
Broad-spectrum diets before farming suggest stress
against: Natufian and early Neolithic populations were small
Hard to show pressure before rather than after farming

positions.claim: Ambitious hosts cultivated cereals for bread and beer to throw feasts and gain followers; domestication began as a luxury.
positions.mech: Competitive feasting rewards surplus production.
for: Göbekli Tepe and other monuments built by foragers
Early domesticates include non-staples
against: Hard to test; feasting leaves ambiguous traces
Staples like wheat dominate early sites

positions.claim: Seasonal climates rewarded storing food; storage and fixed homes made private property enforceable, and property made farming worth adopting.
positions.mech: Institutions, not productivity, explain why farming spread.
for: Early farming was not much more productive than foraging
Storage pits predate domesticated plants
against: Model-based, with thin direct evidence for property norms

positions.claim: Domestication was not an event but thousands of years of tending, harvesting and selecting in rich, stable environments.
positions.mech: Gradual co-evolution of people, plants and animals.
for: Domestic traits in wheat and barley took a millennium or more to fix
Cultivation of wild forms long preceded domestic ones
against: Describes how more than why

state: The field leans to climate as the enabling condition plus slow niche construction; arguments about the trigger continue.
settle: More sites with dated pre-domestic cultivation and storage, compared region by region against climate records, would separate push from pull.
fun: Farming made people shorter, sicker and busier. So why did everyone do it?

name: Why did the first states appear?

positions.claim: States arose where people grew cereals, because grain is visible, ripens at once, stores and can be taxed; early states were fragile tax-collecting machines.
positions.mech: Appropriability of cereal surplus, not productivity, made states viable.
for: Early states grew on cereals, not on roots or tubers
The first writing is accounts of grain and labour
Cross-country data link cereal suitability to early hierarchy
against: Some cereal regions never formed states
Downplays ideology and war

positions.claim: Where farmland was hemmed in by desert, mountains or sea, defeated villages could not flee, so war produced conquest and conquest produced states.
positions.mech: Environmental circumscription plus warfare.
for: Nile valley, coastal Peru and Mesopotamia fit the pattern
Large-scale simulations link warfare to state size
against: Some states arose in open landscapes
War is everywhere; circumscription does a lot of work

positions.claim: Kings grew out of hereditary rank and ritual authority built over millennia in villages and temples.
positions.mech: Ideology and inherited prestige came first.
for: Temples at Eridu rebuilt on one spot for centuries
Ethnographic parallels for rank societies turning into kingdoms
against: Hard to show causation rather than sequence

positions.claim: People lived for millennia in large farming societies without states and switched between forms; states were one experiment among many, not a stage.
positions.mech: Political choice and seasonal variation, not necessity.
for: Trypillia mega-sites of thousands without palaces
Six thousand years between farming and the first states
against: Critics say the book cherry-picks and underrates coercion
Still needs to explain why states won where they did

positions.claim: Irrigated surplus fed specialists (Childe); managing big canals required despots (Wittfogel).
positions.mech: Surplus and water management.
for: Early states sit on irrigated alluvium
against: Mesopotamian canals stayed small and local until after states formed
Hydraulic despotism was shaped by Cold War politics

state: Scott's grain thesis and Carneiro's circumscription are the main live explanations; hydraulic despotism is dead, and Graeber and Wengrow have reopened the question of inevitability.
settle: Systematic regional comparison of when cereal farming, war and hierarchy appear, using datasets like Seshat, would show which comes first.
fun: Writing was invented to count grain and labour. What does that tell you about why the first states were born?

name: Why did new moral philosophies arise across Eurasia around 500 BCE?

positions.claim: In China, India, Iran, Israel and Greece, thinkers independently discovered transcendence and reflected on the human condition: the axis of world history.
positions.mech: Parallel intellectual breakthroughs.
for: Confucius, the Buddha, the Upanishads, the prophets and the Greek philosophers cluster in a few centuries
against: Jaspers named the pattern but gave no mechanism
Zoroaster and Egyptian thought do not fit the dates

positions.claim: Long-literate states let people write, argue and criticise; theoretic culture grew on top of mythic and ritual culture.
positions.mech: Cultural evolution built on literacy and states.
for: All axial centres had long histories of writing and kingship
against: Explains capacity, not timing

positions.claim: When energy capture passed about 20,000 kcal per person per day, people could afford long-term strategies, and ascetic, moralizing doctrines spread.
positions.mech: Rising living standards change psychology and what teachings appeal.
for: A statistical model finds affluence predicts the emergence better than state size or population
The Ganges plain, north China and Greece all boomed before their sages
against: Energy-capture numbers are rough estimates
Seshat analyses find moralizing ideas earlier and elsewhere

positions.claim: Coinage, mercenary armies and slave markets arrived together in the three main axial centres, and the new philosophies answered that world of money and war.
positions.mech: Money's abstraction and market violence shaped new ideas.
for: Coinage appears in Lydia, India and China within about a century
Greek philosophy is full of monetary metaphors
against: Correlation in time is loose
India's and China's coins came after some key thinkers

positions.claim: Moralizing religion and constraints on rulers appear wherever societies become large, from Egypt to the Americas, not in one window of time.
positions.mech: Social scale, not era, predicts axial traits.
for: Seshat coding of many polities finds axial-type traits earlier in Egypt and Mesopotamia
Big gods literature ties moralizing gods to large societies
against: Coding ideas into variables is contested
The cluster of thinkers in 600-300 BCE remains striking

state: Jaspers' pattern is widely used but its explanation is open; Seshat-based work has shifted the burden of proof onto those who see a single age.
settle: Better dating of texts and systematic coding of moral ideas across many more societies, set against measures of wealth and scale.
fun: The Buddha, Confucius, Laozi and Socrates lived within a few generations of each other. Coincidence, money, or something deeper?

name: Why did the Indus cities empty out after 1900 BCE?

positions.school: A weakening monsoon dried the rivers
positions.claim: Summer rains weakened from about 2200 BCE, the monsoon-fed rivers shrank and farmers moved east where rain was steadier.
positions.mech: Less rain, smaller floods, failing flood-recession farming, migration.
for: Lake Kotla Dahar shows abrupt drying around 4100 years ago
River sediments show the Ghaggar-Hakra was monsoon-fed
Settlement shifts east as the rivers fade
against: Cities lasted centuries after the drought began
Proxies are few and far apart

positions.claim: Farmers already coped with variable rain by growing several crops; the urban system dissolved but rural life adapted and continued.
positions.mech: De-urbanization and dispersal as a response to change.
for: Village sites multiply in the east during the Late Harappan
Mixed summer and winter cropping long before the drought
against: Still needs a reason why cities specifically failed

positions.claim: The Gulf trade with Mesopotamia faded and the social order frayed, with rising violence and disease in the late cemeteries.
positions.mech: Loss of elite trade income and social stress.
for: Meluhha disappears from Mesopotamian texts
Head injuries and infectious disease rise at Harappa
against: Trade may have declined as a result rather than a cause

positions.claim: Indo-Aryan chariot warriors destroyed the cities; 'Indra stands accused'.
positions.mech: Conquest.
for: Rigveda describes forts destroyed by Indra
against: The 'massacre' skeletons come from different layers
Ancient DNA puts steppe ancestry in South Asia after the decline
No destruction horizon

state: Climate-driven river change plus adaptation by dispersal is the mainstream view; invasion is dead.
settle: More well-dated lake and cave records from the Indus plains themselves, and excavated Late Harappan villages with dated crop remains.
fun: A civilization bigger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined simply walked away from its cities. Where did everyone go?

name: Why did the Western Roman Empire fall?

positions.claim: The Huns pushed Goths, Vandals and others into the empire; they carved out territories, the tax base shrank, and an emperor without revenue was an emperor without an army.
positions.mech: Migration, lost provinces, lost taxes, lost army.
for: Ammianus records the Huns driving the Goths to the Danube
The loss of Africa in 439 was followed by bankruptcy and the Cape Bon disaster
The empire was not in terminal decline in 375
against: Barbarians were often recruited by Romans
Underplays Roman civil wars

positions.claim: Endless usurpations, court feuds and civil wars spent the army on Romans and drew barbarians in as allies; the barbarian 'invasions' were a symptom.
positions.mech: Political failure at the centre.
for: Civil wars outnumber barbarian wars in the period
Alaric wanted a Roman command
Stilicho stripped the Rhine for internal wars
against: The East had civil wars too and survived
Hard to separate cause from effect in a crisis

positions.claim: The empire rose in a climate optimum and was broken by pandemics and a less stable climate; the Antonine and Cyprianic plagues and the Late Antique Little Ice Age drained its manpower.
positions.mech: Environmental shocks to population, revenue and armies.
for: Ice cores and tree rings show a warm stable optimum then more variability
Lead pollution drops with the Antonine plague
Plague DNA confirms Yersinia pestis in the 540s
against: Critics say the links are correlations of loosely dated series
Mortality figures are guesses
Some papyri show quick recovery

positions.claim: The West changed into a world of kingdoms, bishops and saints; barbarians were accommodated through tax-sharing rather than conquest.
positions.mech: Continuity of elites, law and church.
for: Barbarian kings used Roman law and officials
A creative religious culture flourished
against: Archaeology shows a steep material decline
Downplays violence

positions.claim: The fall was violent and destroyed a complex economy; living standards fell to prehistoric levels in places.
positions.mech: Loss of the state that sustained specialised production and trade.
for: Pottery, coins, roof tiles and cattle size all decline
Britain's economy fell below Iron Age levels
against: Says more about consequences than causes

state: Most historians now combine external pressure with internal political failure; climate and disease are a lively, contested addition, and the 'transformation' school has been pushed back by archaeology.
settle: Better-dated regional series of tax, coin, settlement and mortality data, set against high-resolution climate records, would show which shocks came first and where.
fun: Rome survived Hannibal, civil wars and the third century. Why did Huns, Goths and Vandals finish it in a hundred years?

name: Why did Rome fall in the West but last another thousand years in Constantinople?

positions.claim: A city with water on three sides, a short land front sealed by the Theodosian Walls and cisterns full of water could not be taken by armies without a fleet.
positions.mech: A defensible capital the state could always fall back on.
for: No attacker took the city between 413 and 1204
Huns, Avars, Persians and Arabs all failed before the walls
against: Walls protect a capital, not provinces
The West also had a defensible capital at Ravenna

positions.claim: Egypt, Syria and Anatolia were the empire's richest lands and lay behind the straits; the East could pay for armies and bribes after every defeat.
positions.mech: Revenue kept rebuilding military power.
for: The East paid Attila thousands of pounds of gold and still funded Justinian's reconquest
The West's richest provinces, Africa above all, were the ones lost
against: Revenue figures are estimates
Money did not save the East in the seventh century

positions.claim: Byzantium preferred gold, intelligence and alliances to battle, paying enemies off and turning them against each other.
positions.mech: Avoiding the loss of irreplaceable armies.
for: Tribute to the Huns
Long peace with Persia
Sending Theodoric's Goths to Italy
against: Reads later Byzantine practice back into the fifth century

positions.claim: The Danube front was hard to cross and the Huns, Goths and Vandals found richer, weaker targets in the West; Persia stayed quiet for a century.
positions.mech: Geography and timing of the threats.
for: Attila turned west in 451 after the East stopped paying
The Ostrogoths were sent to Italy in 488
against: Luck is not a mechanism; the East chose to divert threats

positions.claim: In Constantinople emperor, senate, army and people formed a working Roman republic; the court kept control of the army, and the state reorganised itself when disaster struck.
positions.mech: A resilient central state with popular legitimacy.
for: No barbarian generalissimo ever ruled the East
The theme system rebuilt the army after the Arab conquests
against: Constantinople had plenty of riots and coups
Hard to measure legitimacy

state: Historians agree the East's advantages were real: a richer protected tax base, a near-impregnable capital and luckier geography. Recent work adds the strength of its institutions and popular politics.
settle: Comparative fiscal estimates for East and West around 450, and a careful count of where each barbarian group chose to go and why, would weigh money against geography.
fun: Same empire, same laws, same religion, same barbarians: one half died in 476 and the other lasted until 1453. What made the difference?

name: Why did the Han dynasty fall and China split into three kingdoms?

positions.school: Court politics and a broken centre
positions.claim: Eunuch and consort factions, costly frontier wars and the purge of officials hollowed the court; the armies raised against the Yellow Turbans became warlord armies.
positions.mech: Failure at the centre created regional military power.
for: The Proscription of the Partisans
Billions of cash spent on the Qiang wars
Dong Zhuo's seizure of the capital
against: Factional struggles were old; why fatal now?

positions.claim: Local magnates absorbed land and dependants, starved the state of taxpayers and became the base of warlord regimes.
positions.mech: Privatisation of land and power.
for: Registered population fell while estates grew
Warlord armies were built on great-family retainers
against: Census declines may reflect registration, not reality

positions.school: Plague, climate and a religious rising
positions.claim: Epidemics and harsh weather made a healing millenarian movement explosive; the Yellow Turbans broke the dynasty's hold on the east.
positions.mech: Disease and hunger feeding religious revolt.
for: Repeated pestilence recorded from the 150s
The Way of Great Peace healed by confession
against: Climate evidence for the late second century is thin
The rising was crushed within a year

state: Historians stress court politics and the rise of regional military power; the role of epidemics and climate is plausible but poorly measured.
settle: Better-dated climate records for north China in the second century and a fresh analysis of the census and epidemic records would test the environmental case.
fun: Like Rome, Han China fell within two centuries of its peak. Unlike Rome, China came back together. The fall is the same story in different clothes; the comeback is not.

name: Why did the Persian Empire fall to Alexander so fast?

positions.claim: Philip's professional pike-and-cavalry army, under a gifted commander, beat larger Persian armies in pitched battle and fed itself on Persian roads.
positions.mech: Tactical and logistical superiority.
for: Three decisive victories in four years
Macedonian logistics carried the army to India
against: Persia had beaten Greek armies before
Darius came close at Gaugamela

positions.claim: Luxury, harem intrigue and palace murders had rotted the empire.
positions.mech: Moral decay of the court.
for: Bagoas poisoned two kings in two years
against: Artaxerxes III had just reconquered Egypt in 343
The picture comes from Greek writers with an agenda
Achaemenid specialists rejected it in the 1980s

positions.claim: The empire was strong; it fell because the king lost two battles and his nobles abandoned him.
positions.mech: Contingency in battle and noble loyalty.
for: Bessus murdered Darius after Gaugamela
Persian satraps switched sides quickly
against: Hard to separate luck from structural advantage

positions.claim: The empire did not so much fall as change dynasty: Alexander and the Seleucids kept its satrapies, tribute and ideology.
positions.mech: Institutional continuity.
for: Persian nobles kept satrapies
Seleucid administration followed Achaemenid patterns
against: Greek settlers, cities and the burning of Persepolis mark a real break

state: The decadence model is dead; historians weigh Macedonian military excellence against contingency, and many stress continuity after the conquest.
settle: Persian-side sources (Babylonian, Aramaic, Persepolis archives) for the 330s are the key; new finds could show how the satraps chose sides.
fun: The largest empire the world had seen fell in three battles to a 25-year-old. Was it rotten, unlucky, or did it not really fall at all?

name: Why did Meroe fade and Aksum rise?

positions.school: Trade moved to the Red Sea
positions.claim: Roman-Indian trade by sea made Adulis the outlet for African ivory, bypassing the Nile route through Meroe; Aksum grew rich and Meroe poorer.
positions.mech: Shift of trade routes and revenues.
for: The Periplus describes ivory reaching Adulis via Aksum
Aksum struck gold coins for overseas trade
Meroe's Roman trade fades in the third century
against: Meroe's economy was mostly agrarian
Dates of the decline are loose

positions.claim: Aksum's armies under Ezana struck the Nile valley and finished off what was left of Meroitic power.
positions.mech: Military defeat.
for: Ezana's inscriptions describe a Nile campaign
An Aksumite inscription was found at Meroe
against: The inscription may describe a land already in decline
Kings' boasts exaggerate

positions.claim: Meroe faded as new Noba-related groups took over and the kingdom fragmented; it was a slow, local transformation.
positions.mech: Population movement and political fragmentation.
for: Post-Meroitic cemeteries show new burial customs
Continuity of settlement in many places
against: Hard to date the newcomers' arrival

positions.claim: Around Aksum, deforestation and soil erosion undermined the capital's agriculture; at Meroe, iron smelting was blamed for stripping the woods.
positions.mech: Environmental degradation.
for: Slope deposits near Aksum
Huge slag heaps at Meroe
against: New dating does not support catastrophic erosion at the right time
Fuel use at Meroe is not proven to have caused decline

positions.claim: Aksum grew from local highland societies, not South Arabian colonists, and later shifted its centre rather than collapsing.
positions.mech: Indigenous state formation and gradual relocation.
for: Continuity from pre-Aksumite highland sites
Ge'ez and Aksumite institutions develop locally
against: South Arabian influence on early Ethiopian culture is real

state: Most specialists see a shift of trade to the Red Sea and Aksum, plus regional change on the Nile; how far Aksum's armies finished Meroe is still argued.
settle: Excavations dating the last royal phases at Meroe precisely, and more stratified evidence from Adulis, would settle the sequence.
fun: Two African empires traded with Rome; one sold ivory down the Nile, the other by sea. The sea won.
